title: Fast path and allocations
cards/0/body: If the awaiter says IsCompleted = true right away, the method doesn't pause: no subscription, no thread switch, no extra objects. This is the fast path.
cards/1/task: Walk the fast path: the results are already ready.
cards/2/body:
Every async method that pauses creates a heap object: the state machine together with its task.

Ready results can be returned with no allocation: Task.CompletedTask, ValueTask<T>. .NET caches some results itself, such as completed tasks holding true and false.
cards/3/q: A method reads a cache, and 99% of the time the data is there. What should it return?
cards/3/options/0: ValueTask<T>: a cache hit allocates nothing
cards/3/explain: The fast path puts not a single object on the heap.
cards/4/q: Which line is the allocation-free fast path?
cards/4/explain: A ValueTask holding a ready value is a struct; the heap isn't touched.
cards/5/q: Which create no new heap objects? Select all that apply.
cards/5/options/2: await on an already completed task
cards/5/options/3: An async Task method that paused
cards/5/explain: Allocations show up where there is real waiting or new work.
cards/6/q: Can you await the same ValueTask twice?
cards/6/options/0: No: the behavior is undefined; if you need more, call .AsTask() first
cards/7/body: If a method runs millions of times a second, its allocations show up in the profiler. If not, Task is simpler and safer. Optimize after you measure.
cards/7/deep: Since .NET 6 you can mark a method [AsyncMethodBuilder(typeof(PoolingAsyncValueTaskMethodBuilder<>))], and then even a ValueTask method that pauses takes its objects from a pool. Turn it on selectively, after measuring.
cards/8/pairs/1/1: A ready task with a result
cards/8/pairs/2/1: No allocation on the fast path
